ggmtools

Shared tools for R packages that estimate multiple Gaussian graphical models (GGMs), currently

  • spikeyglass: Bayesian joint spike-and-slab graphical lasso (Li, McCormick & Clark 2019), fitted by EM;
  • multiGGM: Bayesian multiple GGMs by MCMC: G-Wishart with a Markov random field prior (Peterson, Stingo & Vannucci 2015), scalable spike-and-slab (scale-multiGGM; Shaddox et al. 2018), multi-platform (Shaddox et al. 2020) and the multiple graphical horseshoe (mGHS; Busatto & Stingo 2025).

Both packages import ggmtools and re-export what users call, so the functions are the same objects whichever package is attached and one downstream script works on fits from either.

Most functions take plain matrices (precision, partial-correlation, score or adjacency matrices) or vectors of p-values and probabilities, not fitted objects. So they work just as well with any other estimator, such as the joint graphical lasso (JGL), the graphical lasso or a random-forest importance score: see Using ggmtools with other methods.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("mljaniczek/ggmtools")

What is in it

What Functions
Shared edge-table format edge_index(), as_pip_table(), diff_edge_table()
Generics with methods in each package pip_table() (long table of PIPs), pcor_estimate() (one partial-correlation matrix per group; ggmtools also provides the method for JGL fits)
Evaluation against a known graph roc_auc(), pr_auc() (tie-correct ROC and PR curves), plot_roc(), confusion_at_threshold() (TPR, FPR, precision, F1, FDR, MCC), topk_overlap()
Estimation error and tuning relative_frobenius(), kl_divergence(), ggm_bic()
Edge selection bayes_fdr() (Bayesian FDR from posterior probabilities), pooled_perm_pvalues() (pooled permutation null)
Matrix utilities precision_to_pcor(), threshold_to_adjacency(), diff_adjacency(), upper_tri_to_matrix()
Data brca_pi3k: TCGA BRCA PI3K-pathway expression, Normal vs Tumor (100 x 28 each)

Example: differential edges in the TCGA data

brca_pi3k holds standardized expression of 28 PI3K-pathway genes in 100 normal and 100 tumour breast samples. With n > p, the inverse sample covariance gives a simple (unregularized) estimate of each group’s partial correlations.

library(ggmtools)

pcor <- lapply(brca_pi3k, function(x) precision_to_pcor(solve(cov(x))))
d <- diff_edge_table(pcor$Normal, pcor$Tumor, threshold = 0.3)
head(d[order(-abs(d$diff)), ])
#>     i  j  node1   node2     est_g1      est_g2       diff
#> 37  2 21 AKT1S1   NPRL3  0.4344316 -0.16654190  0.6009735
#> 33  8 18   MTOR  DEPDC5 -0.1053410  0.47261097 -0.5779520
#> 23  3 15   AKT2    RPS6 -0.5468767  0.02156526 -0.5684420
#> 51 13 24   RHEB PPP2R1A  0.3695557 -0.18810932  0.5576650
#> 47  4 24   AKT3 PPP2R1A  0.3664210 -0.16630078  0.5327218
#> 5   3  6   AKT2 MAPKAP1  0.3845418 -0.14658324  0.5311250

Which of these differences are larger than chance? Permuting the group labels gives a null distribution of |difference|; pooling it over all edges gives fine-grained p-values.

set.seed(1)
X <- rbind(brca_pi3k$Normal, brca_pi3k$Tumor)
diff_score <- function(rows) {
  p1 <- precision_to_pcor(solve(cov(X[rows, ])))
  p2 <- precision_to_pcor(solve(cov(X[-rows, ])))
  abs(p1 - p2)
}
observed <- diff_score(1:100)
null <- replicate(100, diff_score(sample(200, 100)), simplify = FALSE)

pp <- pooled_perm_pvalues(observed, null)
edges <- cbind(diff_edge_table(pcor$Normal, pcor$Tumor, threshold = -Inf),
               pvalue = pp$pvalue, p_adj = pp$p_adj)
head(edges[order(edges$pvalue), c("node1", "node2", "diff", "pvalue", "p_adj")])
#>      node1   node2       diff      pvalue    p_adj
#> 192 AKT1S1   NPRL3  0.6009735 0.004550144 0.604984
#> 144   MTOR  DEPDC5 -0.5779520 0.006507764 0.604984
#> 94    AKT2    RPS6 -0.5684420 0.007380757 0.604984
#> 266   RHEB PPP2R1A  0.5576650 0.008491839 0.604984
#> 257   AKT3 PPP2R1A  0.5327218 0.011851538 0.604984
#> 13    AKT2 MAPKAP1  0.5311250 0.012010264 0.604984
sum(edges$p_adj < 0.05)
#> [1] 0

With 100 samples per group and no regularization, no difference survives the BH correction over all 378 edges. The joint estimators in spikeyglass and multiGGM borrow strength across groups and are the tools to use for a real analysis; the same two calls then test their estimates.

A Bayesian method gives posterior probabilities instead, e.g. P(edge differs). bayes_fdr() selects the largest set of edges whose posterior expected FDR is below a target (tied probabilities are kept together):

prob <- c(0.999, 0.99, 0.97, 0.97, 0.80, 0.40, 0.05)
bayes_fdr(prob, alpha = 0.05)
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE
#> attr(,"expected_fdr")
#> [1] 0.01775
#> attr(,"n_selected")
#> [1] 4
#> attr(,"cutoff")
#> [1] 0.97
#> attr(,"alpha")
#> [1] 0.05

Example: evaluating an estimate against a known graph

In a simulation the true precision matrix is known. Here, a chain graph on 20 variables, estimated from only 40 samples:

set.seed(3)
p <- 20
Omega <- diag(p)
Omega[cbind(1:(p - 1), 2:p)] <- Omega[cbind(2:p, 1:(p - 1))] <- 0.3
X <- matrix(rnorm(40 * p), 40) %*% chol(solve(Omega))

Omega_hat <- solve(cov(X))
score <- abs(precision_to_pcor(Omega_hat))   # edge score: |partial correlation|
truth <- threshold_to_adjacency(Omega, threshold = 0)

roc_auc(score, truth)$auc
#> [1] 0.8024007
pr_auc(score, truth)$auc
#> [1] 0.3226991
cm <- confusion_at_threshold(score, truth, threshold = 0.3)
unlist(cm[c("TP", "FP", "TPR", "FDR", "MCC")])
#>         TP         FP        TPR        FDR        MCC 
#> 11.0000000 23.0000000  0.5789474  0.6764706  0.3478489
kl_divergence(Omega_hat, solve(Omega))
#> [1] 6.767717
relative_frobenius(Omega_hat, Omega)
#> [1] 2.173401

ROC and PR curves step only at distinct score values, so sparse estimators, which tie many edges at exactly 0, get an AUC that does not depend on the order of the variables. For a sparse estimate, also compare pr_auc(..., method = "average_precision"): the default trapezoid draws a straight line across a large tied block, which is optimistic.

sparse <- score * (score > 0.3)      # e.g. a thresholded or lasso-type estimate
mean(sparse[upper.tri(sparse)] == 0) # share of edges tied at 0
#> [1] 0.8210526
c(trapezoid = pr_auc(sparse, truth)$auc,
  average_precision = pr_auc(sparse, truth, method = "average_precision")$auc)
#>         trapezoid average_precision 
#>         0.3188026         0.2854237

Edge tables

Every edge table has the columns i, j, node1, node2 (one row per pair i < j, in upper.tri() order), followed by method-specific columns. pip_table() adds group and pip. Differential-edge tables (diff_edge_table(), spikeyglass::diff_edges()) add est_g1, est_g2, diff and inference columns, using lower/upper for intervals.
